sections.content: This is an excellent introductory economics course highly recommended for social science students. No prior economics knowledge is required. The syllabus covers core micro and macroeconomic concepts, including supply and demand, market structures, economic growth, monetary policy and open economy theories. The curriculum is well-structured and beginner-friendly, avoiding the extreme difficulty of professional ECON courses. It serves as a perfect foundational course for students to build basic economic thinking.
sections.teaching: Professor wang delivers solid and well-organized lectures with extremely clear logic. She explains concepts step-by-step based on course slides with clear emphasis on key and difficult points, without introducing over-syllabus content. The lecture pace is steady and progressive. The professor is responsive and patient with student inquiries, assignment grading and office hour consultations. She is always willing to clarify confusing concepts, making the course accessible for students with zero economics background.
sections.grading:
Closed-book midterm & final; quizzes and problem sets open-book. Strict and transparent criterion-referenced grading
I scored one standard deviation above the mean in both exams and ultimately earned an A.
sections.workload: The overall workload is moderate and student-friendly, ranking as a high-cost-performance elective. No heavy daily workload is required. Students only need to follow weekly lectures and finish assignments on time. Targeted review before exams is sufficient to achieve a good grade. This course balances learning quality and GPA perfectly with much lower pressure than other similar elective courses. Ideal for both GPA boosting and knowledge expansion.

sections.content: The course content is easy to follow, covering basic microeconomics and macroeconomics. Course Description: This course introduces the fundamental theories of microeconomics and macroeconomics. Topics include consumer theory, producer theory, the behavior of firms, market equilibrium, monopoly, the role of the government in the economy, long-run economic growth, the monetary system, and the open-economy macroeconomics.
Intended Learning Outcomes:
On completion of the course, students are expected to be able to:
• Understand the basic logic of economic reasoning;
• Apply basic economic analysis to explain and predict economic relationships;
• Have a deeper understanding of economic issues and events;
• Make critical evaluations on views and opinions related to economics.
Readings:
• The required textbook is Principles of Economics, 6e (2012) by N. Gregory Mankiw,
which is available at the bookstore and also reserved in the library. You are also encouraged to browse the author’s blog (http://gregmankiw.blogspot.com) and read economic and social news.

VIII. Economic growth

XI. Basic concepts of open-economy macroeconomics (if time permits)

sections.content:
The course covers some very basic economics concepts. More specifically, this course is an introduction to macroeconomics.
The course also covers a documentary, 'Inside Job', which is about the 2008 Financial Crisis.
Overall, if you have studied economics in high school, you will have a huge advantage, but it is still possible to do well if you have no prior knowledge in economics--quite a lot of the content can be deduced from common sense, and others require memorization.
sections.teaching:
The professors mainly follows the powerpoint only, so nothing remarkable really happens. Thanks in part to the 'active' participation of the students in class, the lectures tends to be rather boring. In other words, since attendance is not compulsory, it is definitely viable to self-study the contents of this course. (Given that I missed half of the lectures myself, I can verify this).
If I am to attend only 1 lecture for this course, it would probably be the final on 'Inside Job', where he gives a bit more detailed explanation on some of the topics such as leverage, which turns out was covered rather extensively in the final exam. Other than that, since you can watch the documentary on your own, you really do not have to attend the lessons.
sections.grading:
The score calculation is as follow:
Assignment: 16% (You do not need to do all 12 assignments, around 8-9 is ok)
Mid-Term: 34% (You can choose to not attend Mid-Term, then it will not count towards your overall score)
Final: 50% (84% if you choose not to attend the Mid-Term. It is definitely viable--I know people who does this and get good score. It just depends if you want to gamble your entire grade on 1 exam)
The mean, according to the course introduction document, is B-. However, as stated on the document, it is only true 'when in doubt', and the actual mean can be higher or lower. Given the scores shown in Canvas. I would guess the mean is B, but I cannot give a definite answer on that.
sections.workload: The weekly assignments usually consist of around 8 questions from the textbook "Principles on Macroeconomics". The work load is quite heavy...if you take the assignments seriously. However, the TAs probably do not even bother to read your answer, so as long as you hand in something, you will get 2/2 for your assignment. Apparently, some students even directly copy-paste the previous assignment onto the new assignment, and still get 2/2, so yes, you can see how 'seriously' the TAs are.
